newsitem.title: NEPAL: Nepal Marxists move no-trust motion against govt.
newsitem.headline: Nepal Marxists move no-trust motion against govt.

text.p: Nepal's main opposition communist party said on Saturday it was moving a no-confidence motion in parliament against the centre-right coalition of Prime Minister Sher Bahadur Deuba.

"If this government continues further in office the country will have to face a grave situation," former prime minister Man Mohan Adhikary, head of the communist United Marxist Leninist (UML) party told parliament.
"Therefore we have initiated the process of a no-confidence motion to remove it from office."
Deuba's three-party coalition has 108 votes in the 205-member House of Representatives, the lower house of parliament, but is sharply divided.
"The government has not been able to give political stability and the dark cloud of instability is hovering over the Nepali skies," Adhikary said.
Parliamentary officials said the assembly was expected to vote on the motion on Monday.
In September 1995, Deuba's coalition replaced a UML government which held power for barely nine months.

The communists, who failed to remove Deuba in a no-confidence vote last March, are hoping that the Rastriya Prajatantra Party (RPP), the second largest partner in the coalition, will break away from Deuba's Nepali Congress. The RPP has 19 seats and the Nepali Congress has 86.
Seven ministers resigned from the coalition last week but Deuba has accepted only three resignations so far.

The communists have offered to back Lokendra Bahadur Chand, the leader of the RPP's parliamentary wing who is heading the dissident group of his party, as the new prime minister if the motion is passed.
The coalition also includes the three-seat Nepal Sadbhavana Party (NSP), giving it a total of 108 votes against the UML's 87 seats.

Last week the UML moved a motion against Deuba signed by 102 deputies, including 11 from the RPP, two from the NSP and two independents. Under the Nepali constitution the communists need 103 votes to pass it.
The RPP is sharply divided over the issue.
RPP president Surya Bahadur Thapa asked the dissidents on Thursday to defeat the motion against Deuba. Chand told members of the parliamentary party to vote for the motion.
Chand and Thapa, who are longtime political rivals, both claim the support of a majority of their party's 19 deputies.
The uncertainty over the outcome has raised the importance of the small leftist Nepal Workers' and Peasants' party (NWPP), which has three members.
The NWPP has not indicated how it will vote on the no-confidence motion.
Multi-party democracy was established in Nepal, one of the 10 poorest countries in the world, in 1990.
